title: Git Fundamentals
objectives: Understand Git's three areas and the commit graph
Use branches, merges and rebases correctly

sections.markdown: Git is a distributed version control system that tracks changes as a graph of immutable commits, enabling branching, collaboration and history.

sections.code:
working dir --(git add)--> staging --(git commit)--> repo
git status      # what changed
git add -p      # stage hunks
git commit -m   # snapshot
git push        # share

rows: A movable pointer to a commit
Joins histories, creates a merge commit
Replays commits onto a new base (linear history)

sections.markdown: Force-pushing (`git push -f`) to a shared branch rewrites history others rely on. Rebase only your own local/unpushed work; never rewrite shared history.
`git reflog` is your safety net — it records where HEAD has been, so you can recover 'lost' commits after a bad reset or rebase.

flashcards.back: Working directory, staging area (index), and the repository (commits).
Merge preserves history with a merge commit; rebase replays commits for a linear history but rewrites them.
It logs HEAD movements so you can recover commits after a bad reset/rebase.

options: A movable pointer to a commit
quiz.explain: Branches are lightweight pointers to commits — cheap to create.
Rebase replays commits onto a new base, creating new commit hashes.

quiz.q: Safest way to recover a lost commit after a bad reset?
quiz.explain: reflog shows previous HEAD positions so you can restore the commit.

challenges.text: Create a branch, commit, and open a pull request.
Resolve a merge conflict between two branches editing the same file.
Interactively rebase to squash and reorder commits before merging.
Use git bisect to find the commit that introduced a bug.

interviewQuestions: Explain Git's three areas and the staging concept.
Merge vs rebase — when use each?
How do you undo the last commit (keep vs discard changes)?
How do you recover a deleted branch or lost commit?
